prompt.context: Rubber Bumper Co is a small family-owned producer of rubber products. It prides itself on producing a limited range of products but producing the highest quality on the market. In general, new products are introduced after much deliberation and careful market study. The company has recently appointed a new President who noticed decreasing profits over the last couple of years.
prompt.question: Rubber Bumper Co has hired our firm to fix the decline in profits. What are all of the areas that need to be examined in order to identify any major issues that should be a priority?

clarifying_info.q: What type of products does Rubber Bumper sell?
clarifying_info.a: The company only sells two products: rubber bands and condoms.

clarifying_info.q: Is the company seeing similar declines in topline sales?
clarifying_info.a: Topline sales have remained relatively stable over the last 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is Rubber Bumper's market position?
clarifying_info.a: Rubber Bumper is the market leader in both of their product industries.

exhibits.title: Volume sold by competitor (rubber bands and condoms)
exhibits.shows: Two tables showing annual unit volumes for rubber bands (millions of pounds of rubber) and condoms (millions of condoms) from 2011 to 2017, broken out by Rubber Bumper and named competitors plus an 'Others' category, with a total row.

framework: Profits = Revenue - Costs; examine both sides
Revenue: price trends, volume trends, product mix (rubber bands vs condoms)
Costs: variable costs per unit, fixed overhead per factory, cost structure changes
Industry dynamics: market size, growth rate, competitive intensity for each product
Competitive position: market share trajectory vs named competitors in each segment
Internal operations: capacity utilization, factory efficiency, shared vs separate P&Ls

questions.prompt: Question 1: What does Exhibit 1 tell you about the two markets and Rubber Bumper's position?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify: (1) rubber band market is flat/stagnant (~30-31M lbs/yr) while the condom market is growing strongly (~29% from 2011 to 2017, 350M to 450M units); (2) Max Rubber is gaining dominant market share in rubber bands while Rubber Bumper is losing volume; (3) the condom market is more fragmented and smaller players (Others) are capturing disproportionate growth; (4) Rubber Bumper's condom volume grew fast through 2014 then plateaued at 10M units while the total market kept expanding — a great answer proactively flags this stall and asks why.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Compare the financial profitability of the rubber band factory and the condom factory for the most recent year (2017).
questions.guidance: Candidate must convert rubber volume to revenue then compute profit for each factory. Key data to ask for: rubber band conversion rate and variable cost, condom pack price and variable cost. Strong answer arrives at the correct numbers and notes the two profits are similar in absolute terms but condom margins are significantly higher. Great answer also questions why the condom factory overhead is lower despite similar profit.

math.setup: Rubber band factory: 2MM lbs rubber used (from Exhibit 1, 2017). Selling price $20/box of 500 bands; 1 lb = 125 bands; variable cost $1/lb rubber; fixed overhead $4MM/year. Condom factory: 10MM condoms sold (from Exhibit 1, 2017). Selling price $3/4-pack; variable cost $0.10/condom; fixed overhead $2MM/year.
steps: Rubber bands: 2MM lbs x 125 bands/lb = 250MM rubber bands
math.answer: Rubber band factory profit: $4MM. Condom factory profit: $4.5MM. Condom margin (contribution/revenue) is significantly higher: $4.5MM profit on $3MM total costs vs $4MM profit on $6MM total costs.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Should Rubber Bumper convert the rubber band factory to produce condoms? Evaluate financially using a payback period approach.
questions.guidance: A weak answer simply compares $4.5MM vs $4MM profit. A strong answer accounts for opportunity cost of downtime, capex, and computes the incremental annual benefit, then checks against the 4-year payback requirement. Key data to ask for: refurbishment cost ($2MM), 1 year offline, overhead unchanged, bigger plant produces 2x the condom volume of the smaller plant, payback target = 4 years.

math.setup: Cost of project = capex + contribution lost during downtime. Benefit = incremental annual profit from switching. Bigger plant produces 2x the smaller plant's condom volume. Payback = total cost / annual incremental profit. Company threshold: 4 years.
steps: Year offline: contribution lost = Revenue - Variable costs = $10MM - $2MM = $8MM (overhead is a sunk cost)
Bigger plant condom production = 2 x 10MM condoms = 20MM condoms (the smaller plant currently runs at capacity at 10MM)
Bigger plant condom contribution = 20MM x ($0.75/pack price contribution) ... use direct calc: Revenue = 20MM/4 x $3 = $15MM; Variable cost = 20MM x $0.10 = $2MM; Contribution = $15MM - $2MM = $13MM
Incremental annual benefit = $13MM - $8MM = $5MM (overhead is unchanged, so it cancels)
Payback = $10MM / $5MM = 2 years of operation; plus 1 year offline = 3 years total
3 years < 4-year threshold, so the project meets the payback requirement
math.answer: Total project cost is $10MM. Incremental annual profit gain is $5MM. The project pays back in year 3 (1 year offline + 2 operating years), within the 4-year threshold. Recommendation: proceed with conversion.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some of the risks involved with this conversion project?

categories.name: Demand assumptions
ideas: Assumes Rubber Bumper can immediately sell 3x its current condom volume (from 10MM to 20MM units)
Assumes rubber band demand will not rebound; the bigger plant is currently underutilized, implying demand risk

categories.name: Market and competitive risk
ideas: Less diversification: concentrating entirely in condoms increases exposure to a single market
Condoms are not a generic commodity like rubber bands; competing at higher volumes may require significant advertising and brand investment
Smaller fragmented players are capturing most of the condom market growth — unclear if Rubber Bumper can capture share

categories.name: Regulatory and political risk
ideas: Political shifts (e.g., reduced sex education funding) could suppress condom demand
Potentially greater legal and regulatory risk in selling contraception vs rubber bands

categories.name: Operational and execution risk
ideas: 1 year of downtime eliminates rubber band revenue entirely — cash flow impact during transition
Factory conversion may face cost overruns or delays beyond the $2MM / 1-year estimate
Employees may be unwilling or unable to transition to condom manufacturing

recommendation: Convert the rubber band factory to condom production
Financially justified: project cost is $10MM, incremental annual benefit is $5MM, payback is 3 years (within the 4-year threshold)
Strategically sound: condom market is growing ~29% over the study period while rubber band market is flat and Rubber Bumper is losing share to Max Rubber
risks: Most critical risk: demand assumption — Rubber Bumper must be able to sell 20MM condoms vs 10MM today; validate channel and customer demand before committing
Brand and marketing investment will be required to compete at larger scale in the condom market
Complete exit from rubber bands removes all product diversification
next_steps: Conduct customer and retailer interviews to validate demand for 20MM condom units
Develop a marketing and distribution plan to support the volume increase
Negotiate supply contracts to lock in rubber input costs
Stress-test the financial model with scenarios where demand ramp takes 2-3 years instead of immediate
